channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Sandworm and Qilin are inside Cisco firewall management: a critical auth bypass, exploited since August
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 — a critical authentication bypass in Secure Firewall Management Center, patched back in March — has been exploited since August. Crafted HTTP requests reach a process created at boot and hand an unauthenticated attacker root on the appliance that configures your firewalls. Cisco Talos attributes three activity clusters: one deploying a web shell to harvest credentials, one tied to the Russian state group Sandworm delivering Cyclops Blink, and one linked to Qilin ransomware staging encryption target lists. CISA added the flaw to KEV with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, which has now passed. For OT defenders the significance is not the firewall — it is the management plane above it. Whoever holds FMC holds the rule set separating enterprise from plant, and can rewrite it without touching a single controller. - CVE-2026-20079 - Patched Mar 2026; exploitation began Aug 2026; Cisco and Talos disclosure and KEV addition 9 Sep 2026; reported 10 Sep 2026, 6:06 AM ET; KEV remediation deadline 12 Sep 2026, now passed — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 4:00 PM ET

item.title: [High] An industrial automation vendor lost its SCADA/HMI source code — to a public proof-of-concept weaponised within days
item.category: Incident — n-day exploitation campaign; industrial automation, energy, government and election-adjacent targets in five countries
item.description: Acronis Threat Research Unit published findings on 15 September describing a PRC-linked, Chinese-speaking actor it tracks as Red Heron, which turned a public proof-of-concept for a critical Gitea remote code execution flaw (CVE-2026-60004) into an automated mass-exploitation campaign within days of the code appearing. The operators scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and kept a separate list of 477 Taiwan-based systems, classified by target type: defence, energy, aerospace, telecommunications, government, research and election or voting systems. Acronis confirmed compromises at eleven organisations in Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The heaviest loss was a Taiwanese industrial automation company, from which the operators pulled hundreds of repositories including a SCADA/HMI product, surveillance and monitoring software, IoT platform integrations and a network sniffer. - CVE-2026-60004 - Published 15 Sep 2026, 5:11 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector; CISA-quantified scale
item.description: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [High] The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
item.category: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact
item.description: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear. - NBC News reporting on expanded targeting and the State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, as carried by The Record — water-campaign scale from CISA and SecurityWeek - NBC report 2 Sep 2026; $10 million reward announced 3 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] A device manufacturer could not ship for a fortnight — and the plant floor was never touched
item.category: Incident — confirmed production, order and distribution disruption; medical-device manufacturing (global)
item.description: Boston Scientific identified a cybersecurity incident on 25 August 2026 that took down on-premises IT systems across its global operations, disclosed it the following day, and then spent roughly two weeks unable to process or ship customer orders. The company said on 9 September that manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping were fully restored and that product was moving through distribution at or above normal levels while backlogs cleared. Cloud-hosted systems were not affected, no unauthorised activity was found after 25 August, and CrowdStrike was engaged for the response. A separate knock-on effect blocked remote activation of communicators for newly implanted cardiac devices and pairing for new insertable monitors; that was declared resolved on 8 September, and devices already enrolled in remote monitoring continued to function throughout. No compromise of ICS, PLC or process-control systems has been reported. The reason this belongs on an OT page is the shape of the outage rather than its cause: the machines kept running and the company still could not get product out of the door. - Boston Scientific corporate newsroom statements, reported by Cybersecurity Dive, MedTech Dive and TechCrunch - Incident identified 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; remote-monitoring disruption resolved 8 Sep 2026; manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping fully restored 9 Sep 2026 — verified 16 Sep 2026, 12:20 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] Four ways to knock a Siemens edge gateway off the PROFINET segment — and blind SCADA while you do it
item.category: Nozomi Networks Labs research — PROFINET DCP memory corruption in a Siemens OT/IT edge gateway
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published research on 15 September detailing four memory-corruption flaws in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 industrial PC, found using emulation-driven snapshot fuzzing with the Unicorn CPU emulator and AFL++. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578 — an uninitialised-value issue, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads — each carrying a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.3, and affect firmware up to V4.0 HF0. The DCP daemon runs as root, requires no authentication and is bound to all three device interfaces, so an attacker already on the same Layer 2 segment can crash it with crafted Ethernet frames. Siemens has shipped fixed firmware. - CVE-2025-40575 - Published 15 Sep 2026, 5:15 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
item.category: NSA/CISA/FBI/DOE/EPA joint advisory AA26-231A — active targeting of Siemens S7 series PLCs
item.description: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Tenable and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - Published 1 Sep 2026; corroborating reporting 1–2 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] Britain’s NCSC says the same thing for the third time in five months: the exposed box is the way in
item.category: UK NCSC — national-level warning on internet-exposed OT and edge devices; third such warning in five months
item.description: The National Cyber Security Centre published a warning on 1 September that it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, the UK included, by a range of actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The substance is not new and NCSC does not pretend otherwise — it is the third time in five months the agency has pointed at internet-exposed systems and edge devices. What makes it worth reading is the framing of the failure mode: organisations believe their OT is isolated, and it usually is on the architecture diagram, but misconfigurations, unmanaged assets, legacy connections and forgotten remote-access paths quietly undo that. The guidance asks operators to inventory the OT architecture and confirm no PLC or HMI answers directly from the internet. - UK National Cyber Security Centre, reported by GovInfoSecurity and UKAuthority - NCSC publication 1 Sep 2026 — re-verified against current reporting 15 Sep 2026, 10:15 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] An email is now a root shell: Cisco’s mail gateway is being exploited as a zero-day, and it takes no clicks at all
item.category: Cisco Secure Email Gateway (AsyncOS) — CVE-2026-76461, CVSS 9.8, exploited as a zero-day; KEV-listed 14 Sep, federal deadline 17 Sep
item.description: Cisco told customers on Monday that CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in the email-parsing logic of AsyncOS, has been exploited in the wild as a zero-day. A remote, unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted message containing malicious SQL statements; insufficient validation in the parser executes them, ending in arbitrary operating-system commands as root on the appliance. No credentials, no user interaction, no one has to open anything. Both physical and virtual Secure Email Gateways are affected in any configuration; Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 17 September federal deadline. For OT programmes the uncomfortable part is second-order: this is the second Cisco appliance in a week under confirmed attack, and both sit upstream of the enterprise identity your plant network still trusts. - CVE-2026-76461 - Cisco disclosure and KEV addition 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026, 1:18 AM ET; KEV remediation deadline 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS Patch Tuesday reaches the safety controller: a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Schneider’s Modicon M580
item.category: Schneider Modicon M580 / M580 Safety — CVE-2026-3869, CVSS 9.2, not exploited; plus CISA ICSA-26-253-01 (Aveva), 10 Sep
item.description: Schneider Electric, Siemens and Aveva published their September advisories on 8 September, and the one that matters most sits inside a controller family run on safety duty. CVE-2026-3869, rated CVSS 9.2, is an authentication weakness in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety ranges — the mid-tier PLC that runs a great many water, power and process plants, and the same hardware many sites rely on for safety functions. Schneider also fixed high-severity defects in PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, and finally shipped Modicon MC80 patches for weaknesses first disclosed as far back as 2019. Siemens added four critical advisories, including the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay. CISA followed on 10 September with ICSA-26-253-01, the formal advisory for the Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor flaws, which is the only new ICS advisory it published in the last two days. Nothing here is exploited. What makes it consequential is where it lands: on the devices whose failure mode is physical, not informational — and on a patch clock measured in validated outages rather than days. - CVE-2026-3869 - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; roundup published 9 Sep 2026, 6:49 AM ET; CISA ICSA-26-253-01 published 10 Sep 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] The firewall in front of your plant DMZ can be taken with one malformed XML request — root, no credentials
item.category: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS — CVE-2026-0310, CVSS v4 9.2, pre-auth; no confirmed exploitation reported; vendor urgency “highest”
item.description: Palo Alto Networks is telling customers to treat CVE-2026-0310 with its highest remediation urgency. A buffer overflow in how PAN-OS parses XML lets an unauthenticated attacker with network reach to an affected interface write outside the buffer — a denial of service on VM-Series, and arbitrary code as root on PA-Series hardware. Panorama is in scope too. The vendor scores it CVSS v4 9.2; the threat-adjusted CVSS-BT score sits at 7.2 because no exploitation has been observed yet. That gap is the whole planning question. For OT programmes the relevant detail is where these boxes sit: PA-Series hardware is what most sizeable operators use to enforce the Purdue boundary, and Panorama is the console that writes those rules across the estate. Root on the enforcement point is not an IT problem. - CVE-2026-0310 - Vendor advisory published 11 Sep 2026; no exploitation reported — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:15 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The remote-support client your integrator installed can now push and run files on your machine without asking — and it is in KEV
item.category: Advisory — actively exploited remote-support tooling; the software your integrator dials in with
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September with a 14 September federal deadline. The flaw sits in the ConnectWise ScreenConnect client — improper privilege management combined with a missing authorisation check — and it lets files be transferred to and executed on a connected machine through an already-active remote session, without authorisation and without the host confirmation prompt that operators are trained to watch for. CVSS is 9.9. ConnectWise says servers are not affected; the fix is client version 26.6.5. Huntress documented three unrelated incidents in which rogue ScreenConnect installations pushed a malicious VBScript payload to newly connected systems, which is the detail that matters: the abuse path runs from the support platform outward to the endpoint, in the direction integrators and OEMs normally use to reach a plant. - CVE-2026-84869 - Bulletin 8 Sep 2026; KEV addition 11 Sep 2026; reported 12 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 8:15 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The other remote-access box just went live: public exploit code for a NetScaler auth bypass, and attacks the same week
item.category: Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway — CVE-2026-19490, CVSS 9.3, exploitation confirmed
item.description: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 on 19 August — an authentication bypass, CVSS 9.3, in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server, with SAML configurations among those affected. For a fortnight it stayed theoretical. Then public exploit code appeared in early September, and on 3 September sensor operators began recording bypass attempts from multiple source addresses across four countries, with reporting on 4 September confirming attackers had turned to the flaw in the wild. NetScaler is not an OT product, but it is very often the thing an engineer authenticates through before reaching a jump host, a historian or a vendor session — which makes an unauthenticated bypass on it a route to the plant, not merely to the corporate estate. - Citrix security bulletin, corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Help Net Security; exploitation telemetry reported by sensor operators - Patched 19 Aug 2026; exploit code public early Sep 2026; exploitation observed 3 Sep 2026; active targeting reported 4 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 9 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
item.category: MikroTik RouterOS — “MikroTrick” pre-auth SSH takeover chain, confirmed exploited since 2 Sep
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design. - CERT Polska (CSIRT NASK) warning and its companion CVE page, with MikroTik’s September 2026 security bulletin — corroborated by The Hacker News and Security Affairs - Patches released 3 Sep 2026; CERT Polska exploitation warning published 5 Sep 2026 and restated 9 Sep 2026; attacks observed since at least 2 Sep 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] A fourth boundary box in a fortnight: a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the platform your outsourced IT uses to reach every machine you own
item.category: N-able N-central — CVE-2026-86218 (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated remote code execution; exploitation reported
item.description: N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218 on 6 September and rated it CVSS 10.0 — an unauthenticated attacker can execute code on an internet-exposed N-central server, in a low-complexity attack requiring no credentials and no user interaction. The fix is N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4, build 2026.3.1.14, and reporting notes it is the fourth N-central hotfix in roughly five weeks. Huntress reported a compromised production environment but could not establish which of the disclosed flaws was used, and flagged this one as a possible zero-day alongside two high-severity issues; N-able’s own notice describes exploitation observed in the wild. The Shadowserver Foundation tracks close to 1,500 internet-exposed N-central servers, most in the United States and Europe. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform — an agent with system-level rights on every endpoint it manages. For industrial sites, the question is whether the managed service provider that patches your engineering workstations, historians and plant IT runs one, and whether their console is reachable from the internet. - N-able security advisory and incident notice, reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek — KEV listing from CISA’s 8 Sep 2026 catalogue update; exposure count from the Shadowserver Foundation - Disclosed and hotfix released 6 Sep 2026; exploitation reported the same day; added to CISA KEV 8 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 + Rockwell PSIRT — a dozen-plus fixes, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G, read against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index and SecurityWeek’s 2 Sep 2026 round-up of the full Rockwell set - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] The clock has started: anyone selling a connected product into the EU now owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations IN FORCE since 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. As of yesterday, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Industrial Cyber report of 11 Sep 2026 on the reporting rules taking effect, with Freshfields analysis via Lexology - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; reporting obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026; take-effect reporting 11 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:49 AM ET

item.title: [Info] Free tooling for small water systems, in the state that just watched its neighbours get hit — a six-month pilot meant to scale nationally
item.category: Project Watershed 250 — federal/state water-sector cyber pilot, Texas; six months; EPA and CISA as federal partners
item.description: Project Watershed 250 is a statewide pilot connecting Texas water utilities with US cybersecurity vendors at no cost to the utility, over six months, with the stated intent of scaling nationwide if it works. Texas Cyber Command runs implementation; EPA and CISA are the federal partners; Microsoft, Google, Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare are among the providers, with Forescout joining to contribute continuous monitoring, asset visibility and adversary-focused assessment, and Parsons also selected. The timing is not coincidental — it lands while at least a dozen states work through suspected Iranian intrusions into water-sector PLCs. For small systems the significance is blunt: the barrier to basic OT visibility in this sector has always been that a 3,000-connection utility has no security budget, and this removes that argument for six months in one state. - White House and State of Texas announcements, Forescout and Parsons statements, reported by CyberScoop, Nextgov/FCW and Industrial Cyber - Programme announced late Aug 2026; Forescout participation announced 2 Sep 2026 — re-verified 15 Sep 2026, 10:15 PM ET

item.title: [Info] The Department of Energy picks three OT security tools to fund — and all three are aimed at the problem small utilities actually have
item.category: Policy — federal funding for energy-sector OT security tooling; US electric and energy operators
item.description: DOE has selected Frenos, Raptor Dynamix and Bastazo for funding under SENTRY (Securing ENergy Technology ResiliencY), the Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response programme that pushes federally-backed research toward tools energy operators can deploy rather than papers they can read. The three selections cluster around the same bottleneck: not detecting attacks, but deciding what to do with a vulnerability list that nobody has the staff to work through. Frenos builds autonomous OT security assessment; Bastazo, which came out of DOE-funded research at the University of Arkansas, does AI-assisted vulnerability triage and remediation planning for OT, pitched explicitly at cutting a backlog down to the small fraction that carries real consequence. For asset owners the practical significance is not the vendors — it is that the federal funding thesis has shifted from visibility toward prioritisation and remediation, which is where most utility programmes are currently stuck. - US Department of Energy, Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) SENTRY programme — reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 15 Sep 2026 — verified 15 Sep 2026, 8:15 PM ET
